body.p: This paper is filed in response to the Office Action mailed November 22, 2023 (the "Office Action").
Claims 1-8, 18, and 19 are pending in this application. Applicant has amended
claims 1 and 18, and canceled claim 20. No new matter is added by this amendment, and support may be found in the application as filed.
Claim 20 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) as allegedly lacking enabling disclosure.
Claims 1-8 and 18-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly being

indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 112, the applicant), regards as the invention.
Claims 1-8 and 18-20 were rejected under nonstatutory double patenting as
allegedly being unpatentable over claims 1-8 of U.S. Patent No. 11,026,609 to Biederman ("Biederman").
Claims 1-8 and 18-20 were objected to because of certain informalities.
Claims 1-5, 7, and 18-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being
unpatentable over U.S. Patent Publication No. 2010/0324392 to Yee ("Yee") in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2015/0150480 to Zdeblick ("Zdeblick").

Claims 6 and 8 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Yee in view of Zdeblick as applied above and further in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2004/0263264 to Yin ("Yin").
Applicant traverses each of the rejections of the claims and respectfully requests reconsideration and allowance of all claims in view of the amendments above and the remarks below.
I. Double Patenting
Applicant submits herewith a Terminal Disclaimer over Biederman to obviate the double patenting rejection.
II. @ 112 - Claims 1-8, 18, and 19
Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection of claims 1-17 and 23 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly being indefinite. Applicant has canceled claim 20, rendering its rejection moot.
The Office Action asserts

Claim 1 separately defines a biosensor and a second battery, but then recites that part of the biosensor is also part of the second battery. It is unclear how these components are configured - does the biosensor merely comprise most
but not all of the second electrode? How is the biosensor a separate object from the second battery when they have overlapping elements? It appears
that the claim may be describing how the elements are used rather than
defining the structure of the device, but as presented the claim is directed to
an object, not a method, and does not even set forth the object being
"configured to" perform in any particular manner.

Office Action, pp. 5-6. Applicant has amended claim 1 to clarify the relationship between the anode material and the biosensor. In particular, claim 1 now recites, in part, that "the anode material [is] configured for insertion into the subcutaneous layer with the portion of the first electrode, and in combination with the portion of the second electrode, forming a portion of a second battery, wherein the second battery is activatable upon immersion in an electrolytic fluid." Thus, claim 1 recites the constituent parts of a second battery, namely the anode material and the portion of the second electrode. Claim 1 recites that this second battery may then be activated by immersing it in an electrolytic fluid, such as the interstitial fluid in the subcutaneous layer of a person's skin. See, e.g., Specification, ? 20. In view of this, Applicant respectfully asserts that this portion of claim 1 is definite. Claim 18 has been similarly amended and is likewise definite.

Claim 1 was also rejected for reciting that the first battery is "partially electrically decoupled" from the electrodes. Applicant has amended claim 1 to recite that the first battery [is] electrically decoupled from at least one of the electrodes."
All pending dependent claims are definite because their respective independent claims are definite and no independent bases of rejection were raised.
Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 1-8, 18, and 19.
III. @ 103 - Claims 1-8, 18, and 19
Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection of claims 1-17 and 23 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Yee in view of Zdeblick alone or further in view
of Yin.
Yee in view of Zdeblick does not disclose or make obvious an "an anode material

coupled to a portion of the distal end of the first electrode," where the "first electrode" is an electrode of a biosensor, which in combination with the "second electrode" of the biosensor forms a part of a battery. Instead, the Office Action only asserts that Zdeblick discloses battery having an anode material. There are no allegations in the Office Action about placement of the anode material on an electrode of a biosensor or the use of another electrode of the biosensor as another part of a battery. To establish prima facie obviousness of a claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. § 103, the Office Action must show, either from the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill in the art, that the cited references disclose or make obvious each claimed element. See M.P.E.P. §

2143.03; see also Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1 (1966), KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007). Because the Office Action does not cite to any portion of Yee or Zdeblick for these claim elements, the Office Action hasn't stated a prima facie rejection of claim 1. Independent claim 18 recites similar features and therefore the Office Action likewise has not stated a prima facie rejection of that claim either.

In addition, Yee in view of Zdeblick does not disclose or make obvious at least "a wake-up circuit coupled to the second battery to receive a signal from the second battery and, in response, to electrically couple the first battery to the first and second electrodes" as recited in claim 1. The Office Action does not squarely address this claim feature, but instead drops the "second battery" in favor of a mechanical switch. Office Action, p. 7. Claim 1 recites a "wake-up circuit" that receives a signal from "a first battery" and "in response, [] electrically couple[s] the second battery to the first and second electrodes." Yee in view of Zdeblick is entirely devoid of any teaching to use one battery to activate a second battery. Thus, the rejection is incorrect.

As mentioned above, Yee employs a mechanical switch to activate its device, not a signal from a battery. See, e.g., Yee, j7 131, 136, 137. Further, Yee's device is not activated based on insertion into an electrolytic fluid. It is activated when the mechanical switch is closed, irrespective of any other condition. Thus, nothing in Yee suggests activating the
device by using a signal from another battery that is based on insertion into an electrolytic fluid.

Zdeblick likewise does not have any such teaching. Instead, Zdeblick uses its battery to power its device. It has no "wake-up circuit" or switch or any other electrical circuit that couples one battery to its electrodes in response to a signal from another battery and there is nothing in the record to suggest reconfiguring the Yee device to include Zdeblick's battery as a replacement for Yee's mechanical switch.

Thus, Yee in view of Zdeblick does not disclose or make obvious "a wake-up circuit coupled to the first battery to receive a signal from the first battery and, in response, to electrically couple the second battery to the first and second electrodes." Therefore claim 1 is allowable over Yee in view of Zdeblick for these additional reasons.

For at least these reasons claims 1 and 18 are allowable over Yee in view of Zdeblick. Dependent claims 2-8 and 19 are each allowable at least based on their dependence from an allowable independent claim.
Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 1-8, 18, and 19.
Applicant respectfully asserts that in view of the amendments and remarks above, all pending claims are allowable and Applicant respectfully requests the allowance of all claims.
